# Types of User

> "God, I thank you that I am not like the rest of men"
>
> — a Pharisee at prayer, Luke 18:11

Men who do it every day tend to envy the man who doesn't. We've all met him, or read his posts. "Honestly, I can go a couple of weeks and not even think about it." We wish we were built like that.

Don't. This may be hard to believe, but no man in the trap enjoys being in it, however lightly he seems to wear it. Keep three things in view:

- No man ever decided to become a user, light or heavy.
- So every man in the trap feels like a fool.
- So every man in the trap has to lie, to himself and to everyone else, to make it look like a choice.

A pastor who has written on this noticed the same thing about the men who come to him: "Their masturbation isn't a calculated moral decision; it's a compulsion."

Think about how people talk about things they really enjoy. A keen fisherman tells you how often he gets out on the water, and wishes it were more. So why does a man boast about how *little* he jerks off? If going without is the thing to be proud of, the trophy belongs to the man who never does it at all.

Suppose a friend said to you, "I can go a whole fortnight without toast, and it doesn't bother me in the slightest." You'd wonder what was wrong with him. If he likes toast, why go without? If he doesn't, why mention it? A man only makes a speech like that about something that has a hold on him. What the light user is really telling you is: "I survived two weeks." Like every man in the trap, he's hoping that if he can survive two weeks he might one day survive for good. And if two weeks was a feat of survival, imagine how precious the next time must have been.

That's why the light user is, in one way, more firmly caught than the heavy one. The illusion of pleasure is bigger for him, because he's always coming off a long wait. He also has less reason to get out. It costs him less time, and the damage is harder to see. When something does go wrong, such as a flat mood, a wandering mind in bed with his wife, or a coldness when he tries to pray, he puts it down to work or tiredness or his age.

Remember what the "pleasure" is. It's the end of an itch that the habit itself put there. The Little Monster is so small that most of the time we don't know he's with us.

## Why every man doesn't do it all day {-}

If you've got an itch that never quite goes, the natural thing is to scratch whenever it nags. Since each scratch works a little less well than the one before, the natural drift is always towards more: more often, for longer, with stronger material. So why isn't every man in the trap doing it five times a day? Four things hold him back.

1. **Time.** He has a job, a family and a life, and most days are full.
2. **The body.** It has limits. A man can only go so many rounds, and those limits change with his age, his health and how tired he is. It's an automatic brake.
3. **Privacy.** A wife in the bed, a roommate, children who don't knock, thin walls. For many men the only thing between them and twice as often is a lack of locked doors.
4. **Conscience.** The tug of war that goes on in every man in the trap. Some of it comes from church, some from a wife's opinion, and some from a plain dislike of what he's turning into.

Heavy users tend to think of themselves as weak, and can't see how other men keep it to once a week. But the once-a-week man is usually no stronger. One or more of those four brakes is simply on harder. He shares a small flat, or he's fifty-five, or he works fourteen-hour days. Take the brake off, say with a week alone in a hotel, and watch what he does.

Now some definitions.

## The man who never started {-}

He does exist, though he's rare, and he shouldn't be smug about it. He's outside the trap by upbringing, luck or the grace of God. Every man inside it was once sure he'd never be caught, and some men stay "outside" for years by trying it only now and then, which is how all the rest of us began.

## The light user {-}

There are two sorts.

**The beginner.** He has fallen in and doesn't know it yet. He's usually a boy of twelve or thirteen, though it can happen to a grown man at any age. Don't envy him. He's a fly strolling about on the rim of the jar, and in all likelihood he'll be doing it nightly within a year or two. Every nightly man started out as an occasional one.

**The man who used to be heavier and believes he can't stop altogether.** He's the saddest of all, and he comes in several varieties. Each needs a word of its own. Find yourself in the list. You may be in it more than once.

## The nightly sleep aid {-}

Once a day, in bed, lights off. He calls it his sleeping pill.

Ask him two questions. If he enjoys it so much, why only once? And if it means so little to him, why do it at all?

We dealt with "I can't sleep without it" a few chapters back. Here, look at the arithmetic. The nightly man eases his itch for perhaps ten minutes in every twenty-four hours. He doesn't notice it, but for the other twenty-three hours and fifty minutes he's carrying the itch around with him. He's walking all day with a stone in his shoe so that he can enjoy taking it out at bedtime.

He keeps it to once because of the brakes: he has a wife, or a job to get up for, or a conscience that would start to shout at twice. It's fairly easy to show a five-a-day man that he isn't enjoying himself. He often knows already. The once-a-night man is harder to persuade, because his one time comes at the end of a whole day's wait and so it feels like a comfort.

## The married man {-}

He thought the wedding would end it. Many of us did. He found out within the month that it had come with him on the honeymoon.

He believes he's owed a release every day or two, and his wife is not always of the same mind. She's tired, or pregnant, or away, or they've had a row. So he "fills the gap". But the habit doesn't stay inside the gap. Soon it's happening on nights when she would have said yes, because it's quicker, because it asks nothing, because nobody has to be wooed. In time he's half glad when she turns over, since it hands him his excuse. Some men will even pick the quarrel that produces the excuse.

And when she does reach for him, he's already spent, or his mind is on a reel she isn't in. He gave the best of it to nobody, and she gets what's left over.

If the habit really gave a man so much, he wouldn't need a wife. It gives nothing, and it takes from her. One husband wrote, after he finally saw it:

> "I was beside myself over how I had grieved God and my wife"
>
> — a married man on a Christian recovery blog

Whatever you believe about marriage, you promised her this part of yourself. A man who takes it back in secret, a little at a time, is a man she can't fully trust, and some part of her knows it even if she couldn't tell you what's wrong.

## The streak counter {-}

His motto: "Stopping is easy. I've done it dozens of times."

You met him in the chapter on willpower. Twenty days on, a fall, a reset, a new vow, and thirty days on. He has an app, or a row of crosses on a calendar. The heavier user envies him. "At least he gets a month clean at a time."

But look at what his life is like. When he's doing it, he wishes he weren't. When he's stopped, he feels deprived and counts the days. Then he falls, hates himself, and wishes he hadn't. He never gets to enjoy either state. He has the worst of both.

It's worth noticing that this is true of every man in the trap. When you're free to do it, you either do it without noticing or you wish you didn't. It only becomes precious when it's forbidden. That's the forbidden-fruit problem, and a man can't win at it, because the thing he's pining for was never there. There's only one way to stop pining for it, and that's to see that it's empty.

A cousin of the streak counter is the retention monk. He's stopping in order to get something: a deeper voice, a glow, a magnetism that will turn women's heads. He isn't free either. He has only swapped one kind of counting for another, and when the superpowers fail to arrive on schedule he's back where he started with a grudge. More on him in a later chapter.

## "Porn-free but still doing it" {-}

This may well be you, since this book is a sequel. You got out of the harem, and you're rightly glad. But the hand stayed.

You tell yourself it's a different thing now. "It's natural. There's no screen. It's just a body doing what bodies do." So ask yourself what your mind is doing while your body does it. Remember the man in the introduction who'd quit porn twice and gone back twice. Both times, this was the door he went back through.

The porn-free user is living on a ration, exactly as the chapter on cutting down described. He has cut out the worst of it and kept the engine running. He's still feeding the same Little Monster, who was never fussy about where his meals came from. And on some bad night, when the memories have worn thin, the monster will remember where the stronger food is kept.

## The "imagination only" user {-}

"I don't look at anything. It's all in my head."

Everybody starts there. Isn't it strange how the scenes don't stay tame? Last year's picture stops working, so the mind supplies something a little further on. Then it wants a real face: a colleague, a friend's wife, the girl who serves your coffee. Then it wants "just a photo, to get started". We traced that road in the chapter on the flesh.

Even FitXFearless, who will tell a desperate man that his own imagination is the lesser evil compared with a screen, won't call it good: "Both of them are bad." And of imagination: "It's not that much better."

Two scholars who studied the question for a theological journal put it flatly: "in the vast majority of cases, masturbation involves lustful thoughts." You knew that already. The imagination-only man is proud that no one else's sin is on his screen. But he's the director, the casting agent and the whole audience of his own private cinema, and the women in it never agreed to appear.

Worst of all is the husband who believes he's safe because he only ever pictures his wife. He's still teaching his body that the finish line is himself, alone, on his own timetable, with a version of her who never says "not like that" and never needs anything. Then he's puzzled that the real woman feels like harder work than she used to.

The next chapter is all about the thought life, so we'll leave him there for now.

## The church guy who has never told anyone {-}

He serves on the welcome team, leads a small group, perhaps plays in the band. He has done this since he was fourteen and has never said one word about it to a living soul.

On Sunday he's at the front with his hands raised. On Saturday night he was where he always is. He has confessed it so many times, in the same words, that he's embarrassed to bring it up with God again. So he's stopped bringing it up, and after a while he's stopped bringing much else up either. One man wrote down what that feels like from the inside:

> "I Feel Dirty When I Go Before God And Am Losing My Self"
>
> — a commenter on a Christian recovery blog

It leaks into everything he might have done. He turns down the mission trip, lets someone else lead, and never says why.

The church guy has one burden the others don't. He believes he's the only one. He looks down the row at the other men and assumes they're all clean. They're looking back down the row at him and assuming the same. The habit is feeding on that silence, and there's a whole chapter on it shortly.

## "I'll stop when I'm married" {-}

He's single, and he has a plan. The habit is a stopgap. Once there's a ring and a real woman, he won't need it, and it will drop away without any effort.

Ask the married man two sections up how that went.

The habit was never about not having a woman. It's about ending an itch, and a wedding doesn't end the itch. What he'll bring to his marriage is ten or fifteen years of training in sex that is instant, solitary, silent, and entirely about himself. Then he'll be asked to do the opposite, with a real person, who has moods of her own. Even James Dobson, who took about the softest line on this habit of any well-known Christian teacher, listed carrying it into marriage among his worries.

"When I'm married" is also the most comfortable way there is of saying "not yet". It sounds like a plan, and all it does is put the day off. If you intend to give a woman your whole self one day, the kindest thing you can do for her is to arrive already free.

## A week in the life of a ration {-}

All these men make one mistake about each other. Each assumes that the man who does it less is happier and more in charge. He may be more in charge. He isn't happier.

To see why, don't take anyone's word for it. Just picture a Saturdays-only man and follow him through a week.

On Sunday he's low and a bit ashamed, and also relieved, because the next one is as far off as it will ever be. By Tuesday the itch has started, and he's less patient with the children than he meant to be. On Wednesday night he lies awake. He used to sleep straight after; now he's wide-eyed at one in the morning, thinking about Saturday. On Thursday he's distracted at work. On Friday his wife suggests having friends over tomorrow evening, and he hears himself snap at her, and can't explain it, and apologises.

On Saturday he's planning from lunchtime. He works out when the house will be empty. If the plan is threatened, he gets irritable out of all proportion. When the time comes he doesn't just get on with it. He's waited a week, so it has to be worth it. He dwells on it and draws it out, because this one has to carry him through seven more days.

Ten minutes later he's sitting on the edge of the bed feeling exactly as he did last Saturday.

Is that man in control of anything? Outwardly he's the disciplined one, the once-a-week man the daily user envies. Inwardly he has spent six days out of seven in a quiet fight, and the seventh losing it by appointment. And the logic of his position doesn't hold. Either there's something real in the habit or there isn't. If there is, why wait a week for it? If there isn't, why do it at all?

He doesn't have to be a weak man. He may well be a strong one. It takes real discipline to live like that, year after year. That's what's so sad about it. He's spending the strength of a soldier on guarding a ration of nothing.

If you're thinking, "That's an exaggeration, I'm nothing like that," be careful. You have been that man for a day or two at a time, every time you tried to hold out.

AND THE GAPS ONLY GET SHORTER.

## We all lie about it {-}

Men in this trap are liars, and we lie to ourselves first. We have to. Almost every light user does it more often, and on more occasions, than he'd admit. Sit the "twice a week" man down and go through his last seven days honestly, and you'll find it was four times, plus one he'd decided didn't count.

Read the forums, and you'll see what the light users are really doing. They're counting days, or they're waiting to fail. Not one of them is at ease.

You don't need to envy any of them, and you don't need to be one. Life is simply better outside. Here is a man who got out:

> "From that moment on, I began rejoicing that Jesus had delivered me from this 5 year addiction"
>
> — a 19-year-old man, in a testimony on a Christian site

He didn't write that he was managing it, or that he'd reached day ninety. He wrote that he'd been delivered, and that he was rejoicing.

Which brings us back to the Pharisee at the top of the chapter. He stood in the temple and thanked God that he wasn't like other men. Every type in this chapter says a version of that prayer. "At least I don't look at porn." "At least it's only once a week." "At least it's only in my head." "At least I'm not married yet." Jesus said the man who went home right with God that day was the other one, the one who didn't compare himself with anybody.

There aren't really seven types. There's one trap, and men are standing at different depths in it. The way out is the same for all of them.

## A word about boys {-}

Teenagers are the hardest to reach. It isn't any harder for them to stop. They just don't believe they're caught. A boy of fifteen is at the shallow end, and he's sure he'll climb out long before it matters, at university, or when he gets a girlfriend, or when he's married. You've just read how that goes.

If you're a father, don't take comfort from the fact that your son is a good lad who goes to youth group. So were you. Don't rely on a scare talk either, because the trap hasn't changed since you fell into it. He doesn't need frightening. He needs someone who has been there to tell him the truth early: what it is, how it catches you, and that there's nothing in it. There's more on that later in the book.
